tagline: No-code automation platform connecting thousands of apps.
verdictSummary: A handful of personal automations — this webhook triggers that API call — is a real weekend build, running as plain code instead of a visual flow. What doesn't come with it is Zapier's actual product: a catalog of thousands of pre-built, maintained integrations, most of which need OAuth flows this build deliberately does not attempt.
coreLoopDIY: A small automation runner: each pipeline is a scheduled job or a webhook handler that calls a couple of APIs directly, with every run logged and retried on failure.
whatYouLose: the pre-built integration catalog for thousands of apps
OAuth connections maintained on your behalf
run history and retries handled for you
whyPeopleStillPay: Every new app connection Zapier offers is already built, authenticated, and kept working as that app's API changes — people pay to skip writing and maintaining that integration code themselves.
notes: A structural 'kinda': any single automation is an easy build, but Zapier the integration network is not.
prompt:
Build a personal automation runner for the handful of pipelines you actually use — not a general integration platform. Each pipeline is plain code: a trigger (a cron schedule or a webhook endpoint with a per-pipeline secret token) and a handler that calls the APIs it needs directly. Log every run to a database — pipeline name, trigger payload, status, duration, error — and retry a failed run a few times with backoff before giving up; notify yourself after the final failure. Build a small admin page showing recent runs with their status and a way to inspect or re-run one. Adding a new pipeline should mean writing a short script, not hunting for a pre-built connector.

Do not build OAuth flows for third-party apps, or any kind of integration catalog or visual builder — restrict pipelines to services with simple token-based API keys, stored in the environment and never committed. A service that only offers OAuth is genuinely more setup work per integration; that ongoing maintenance across thousands of apps, not any single automation, is what the subscription buys.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Zaps?
faq.a: Not automatically — Zapier's visual flows don't export to code. Each Zap you actually rely on becomes a short script you write by hand, which for most personal automations is a handful of pipelines, not hundreds.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: The admin page for checking run history works in a phone browser, but pipelines themselves run unattended on a server — there's nothing to interact with on mobile day to day, which is roughly how Zapier works too.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month, regardless of how many pipelines you run — no per-task pricing tiers to think about.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: OAuth-based integrations. Any service that requires signing in with your account instead of a plain API key is out of scope here; that's most of Zapier's most popular app connections, and building each one by hand would cost real time per app.
